body.heading: Small words, big rescues
paragraphs: Every Scrabble player knows the pain of a rack holding Q with no U in sight. The rescue is a family of tiny, unlikely words that tournament players memorise first. Qi (pronounced “chee”) is the life force in Chinese philosophy — and a legal play that parks your Q on a triple-letter square.

Za is slang for pizza, and just as legal. Xu was a Vietnamese coin, jo is a Scots word for a sweetheart, and ka names a spirit in ancient Egyptian belief. None of them will win a poetry prize, but each can win a turn.

body.heading: Why two letters matter
paragraphs: Scrabble boards fill up fast, and most late-game plays are short words threaded through gaps, scoring in two directions at once. Knowing the two-letter words — there are over a hundred in the official lists — turns blocked positions into scoring chances.

They also rescue the vowels. A rack of five vowels looks hopeless until you remember ai (a three-toed sloth), oe, ea and the humble aa, a kind of rough lava. In Scrabble, no rack is truly dead; it is only unread.

body.heading: Try it: the two-letter drill
paragraphs: Write ten two-letter words on cards — qi, za, xu, jo, ka, ai, oe, aa, xi, om — with the meaning on the back, and quiz each other while dinner cooks. Xi, by the way, is a Greek letter; om is the sacred syllable.
Then play a game with one house rule: any player may, once per game, swap a single tile instead of taking a turn. You will find the tiny words matter even more when every tile counts.

takeaway: In Scrabble, the shortest words do the heaviest lifting: learn qi and za and the letter Q becomes a gift instead of a curse.
